cells.tense: You are standing where the whole arc finally shows its shape, and you know it.
cells.ask: Name one thing that's finished — out loud, to someone who watched you do it — and say what it opened, not what it closed.
cells.core:
You can see how the pieces fit while you're still inside the thing. Most people manage one of those at a time. When a stretch comes to its end, you notice the ending, and you don't slam the door — you let the next thing in. That's not detachment. You're still in it, just not lost in it.

The door is open because you opened it. So when you talk about the work ahead, you talk about the work ahead, not about how long the last part took. And when someone brings you a problem, the first thing you reach for is the shape of it, not the tactics. You're standing in the turning, and you can feel it turning.
cells.sheetLine: You see the whole shape, and you let it close.
cells.verb: Bringing a long arc to its close and letting it open into the next.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it.

cells.tense: You have already called this finished in your head, and the ending is not here yet.
cells.ask: Pick whatever you've been treating as done and tell one person what's still open in it. Then take the next real step — the email, the call, the page — without announcing it.
cells.core:
You're standing at the end of something before it's ended. In conversation you sum up like the story's over — you've learned the lesson, you've got the takeaway, you're ready for what's next. But the thing still has a room or two you haven't walked. Declaring arrival is a way of not having to be in the unfinished part, and the unfinished part is where the work actually is.

What you've lost isn't the vision. It's the present tense. You read the thing as already over while it's still going. People around you can feel the difference between someone who's lived the conclusion and someone who's skipped to it — and they're waiting for you to come back into the room, not to the next one.
cells.sheetLine: You've called it done. It hasn't finished yet.
cells.verb: Bringing a long arc to its close and letting it open into the next.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it.

cells.tense: You were at a door a while back that has already closed behind you, and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Ask one person who was there at the start of a thing you finished what they saw you do. Let them answer fully, then write one line of what you heard.
cells.core:
The arcs keep not closing for you. You start things, and when they get near the end you find a reason to keep them open — one more revision, one more question, one more angle. The whole pattern is right there and you won't step out of the room to look at it. It isn't that you can't see. It's that seeing would mean the thing is over, and you've been treating over as a loss.

So everywhere you look there are loose ends. The ability to see the pattern is still in you — it just has nowhere to land while nothing is allowed to end. You don't need more insight. You need one thing to actually be done.
cells.sheetLine: You won't let anything end, so nothing gets to start.
cells.verb: Bringing a long arc to its close and letting it open into the next.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it.

cells.tense: You are already letting a finished thing go, and you are describing it as something that happened to you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been saying fell away or ran its course, and say instead: that was mine to end. One sentence, to one person, today.
cells.core:
Something in your life has already closed, and you keep talking about it as if it decided itself. You say it ended, it ran out, people moved on — as though the cycle moved without you. But you were the one who stopped returning the call, who stopped opening the file, who let the last meeting be the last. That was a choice, and it was yours.

The easing-out is already happening through your hands. You just haven't owned it. The part you won't claim is why it feels like something is unfinished when nothing is — you're carrying a decision you won't admit you made. Say it out loud, plain, and the weight changes shape. Not because the loss gets smaller, but because it becomes yours, and yours can be set down.
cells.sheetLine: You let it go. You keep saying it fell away.
cells.verb: Bringing a long arc to its close and letting it open into the next.
cells.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it.

attempts.check: The draft's one unsupported claim is that this person is standing at a specific completed cycle they have not named; the record only knows cycles close and the person may genuinely be mid-journey rather than past the door. A reader could object that seeing the whole pattern is just what anyone does when they step back, not a distinct capacity — so the cells describe how the capacity is bending here, not proof it is present. The asks survive being wrong: each one is a concrete act a camera could see, useful whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves the writer is 'the cycle closes' — it sounds wise and costs nothing; I have replaced it with what the person could check.
